newsitem.title: ITALY: OLYMPICS-FIS WARNS OF NAGANO "TERRORIST" THREATS.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-FIS WARNS OF NAGANO "TERRORIST" THREATS.

text.p: Japanese environmental groups have said they will attack the 1998 Nagano Winter Olympics if the men's downhill starts inside a national park, the world skiing body said on Wednesday.

Marc Hodler, the president of the International Ski Federation (FIS) and himself an International Olympic Committee (IOC) vice-president, told Reuters that the local organising committee had received threats of violence.

"We have been told that there are threats, that if we impose a higher starting point that groups have informed the organising committee that they will attack the Games in a terrorist way," Hodler said at the Alpine skiing world championships.
"This is a responsibility that the IOC does not want to have, neither do FIS," he added.
He said the FIS had not given up hope of getting what they wanted. "There is still a possibility that we can find an agreement with those groups," he said.
"The Olympics are, as you know, a theatre. A very much appreciated theatre for whatever opposition there is going, from protests to demonstrations to terrorist acts."

Terrorism has long been the major nightmare of Olympic organisers, from Munich in 1972 when Palestinian guerrillas shot dead 11 Israeli athletes to the bombing which shook the Atlanta Summer Games last year, killing two people.
That bombing still remains unsolved.
Francois Carrard, the IOC director general, said earlier in Nagano that his organisation would not push the local organisers to lengthen the men's downhill course.
"We respect totally the concerns for the local environment and the IOC is never going to force anything upon NAOC (Nagano Olympic Organising Committee) in that area," he said.
The FIS wants to raise the start of the downhill in Hakuba, 50 kms west of Nagano, to 1,800 metres above sea level to lengthen the run and include a spectacular jump.
That would affect parts of the national park.
The world body has offered to run the race from the higher start point without the usual permanent structures.

Both CBS, the American network which paid a record $375 million for the U.S. broadcasting rights to the Nagano Games, and Seiko, the official timer, have said they do not need permanent buildings at the start.
But local organisers have refused to countenance a higher start, saying permanent structures are needed.
They also say there is a pond separating the proposed higher area from the lower course they want adopted.

Gianfranco Kasper, secretary general of the FIS, suggested earlier at the world championships that a major reason for the local organisers' determination to have their way was that they would lose face if they gave way.

He said the Nagano organisers had promised the environmental groups when they first bid for the Games that the national parks would not be used and would lose face if they backtracked over the downhill start.

Bernhard Russi, the Olympic downhill course designer, confirmed there was a pond where the local organisers said but added that in winter it was completely solid and that some 10,000 tourists skied over it daily in that period.
He said the piste barely encroached into the national park, mostly running alongside it rather than in it on the upper parts: "Its just a matter of a few little bits of it."
He said that the tree line ended at around 1,400 metres above sea level, so trees would not be endangered.
"All this discussion makes me very sad because people start thinking that the downhill course is not good," he added. "In fact it is excellent and all the skiers agree."
